claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Costa-Mattioli and Monteggia, 2013; Lipton and Sahin, 2014.

claims.claim: It is currently unclear how mTOR activation might be controlled at specific synapses and linked to mechanisms that gate learning and memory.
claims.source: However, it is currently unclear how mTOR activation might be controlled at specific synapses and linked to mechanisms that gate learning and memory.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: NMDARs contain multiple subunits, including an obligatory GluN1 subunit, various GluN2 (A–D) and, for some subtypes, one of the GluN3 (A–B) subunits.
claims.source: NMDARs contain multiple subunits, including an obligatory GluN1 subunit, various GluN2 (A–D) and, for some subtypes, one of the GluN3 (A–B) subunits (Paoletti et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about NMDAR composition, supported by citation to Paoletti et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Conventional NMDARs containing GluN1 and GluN2 trigger gene expression programs that mediate the strengthening and stabilization of active synapses and the persistent storage of information.
claims.source: Conventional subtypes containing GluN1 and GluN2 trigger gene expression programs that mediate the strengthening and stabilization of active synapses and the persistent storage of information (Lyons and West, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Lyons and West, 2011.

claims.claim: Nonconventional NMDARs containing the GluN3A subunit inhibit many synaptic modifications.
claims.source: By contrast, nonconventional subtypes containing the GluN3A subunit (GluN3A-NMDARs) inhibit many of these synaptic modifications (Pérez-Otaño et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Pérez-Otaño et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Synapses that express GluN3A are resistant to the induction of long-lasting functional and structural plasticity.
claims.source: Synapses that express GluN3A are resistant to the induction of long-lasting functional and structural plasticity, and memories fade more quickly in mutant mice with enhanced GluN3A expression (Kehoe et al., 2014; Roberts et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Kehoe et al., 2014; Roberts et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Memories fade more quickly in mutant mice with enhanced GluN3A expression.
claims.source: Synapses that express GluN3A are resistant to the induction of long-lasting functional and structural plasticity, and memories fade more quickly in mutant mice with enhanced GluN3A expression (Kehoe et al., 2014; Roberts et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Kehoe et al., 2014; Roberts et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Human genetic studies correlate enhanced cognitive performance with low GluN3A levels or variations in GRIN3A.
claims.source: In line with this work in mice, human genetic studies correlate enhanced cognitive performance with low GluN3A levels or variations in GRIN3A (human gene encoding GluN3A) (Gallinat et al., 2007; Papenberg et al., 2014; Sadat-Shirazi et al., 2019); and GluN3A dysregulation in humans is linked to cognitive impairment in schizophrenia (Greenwood et al., 2019; Mueller and Meador-Woodruff, 2004; Ohi et al., 2015; Takata et al., 2013), Huntington's disease (Marco et al., 2013; Marco et al., 2018), addiction, and other pathologies (Huang et al., 2017; Pérez-Otaño et al., 2016; Sarker et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2015; Yuan et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Gallinat et al., 2007; Papenberg et al., 2014; Sadat-Shirazi et al., 2019.

claims.claim: GluN3A dysregulation in humans is linked to cognitive impairment in schizophrenia.
claims.source: In line with this work in mice, human genetic studies correlate enhanced cognitive performance with low GluN3A levels or variations in GRIN3A (human gene encoding GluN3A) (Gallinat et al., 2007; Papenberg et al., 2014; Sadat-Shirazi et al., 2019); and GluN3A dysregulation in humans is linked to cognitive impairment in schizophrenia (Greenwood et al., 2019; Mueller and Meador-Woodruff, 2004; Ohi et al., 2015; Takata et al., 2013), Huntington's disease (Marco et al., 2013; Marco et al., 2018), addiction, and other pathologies (Huang et al., 2017; Pérez-Otaño et al., 2016; Sarker et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2015; Yuan et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Greenwood et al., 2019; Mueller and Meador-Woodruff, 2004; Ohi et al., 2015; Takata et al., 2013.

claims.claim: GluN3A dysregulation in humans is linked to cognitive impairment in Huntington's disease.
claims.source: In line with this work in mice, human genetic studies correlate enhanced cognitive performance with low GluN3A levels or variations in GRIN3A (human gene encoding GluN3A) (Gallinat et al., 2007; Papenberg et al., 2014; Sadat-Shirazi et al., 2019); and GluN3A dysregulation in humans is linked to cognitive impairment in schizophrenia (Greenwood et al., 2019; Mueller and Meador-Woodruff, 2004; Ohi et al., 2015; Takata et al., 2013), Huntington's disease (Marco et al., 2013; Marco et al., 2018), addiction, and other pathologies (Huang et al., 2017; Pérez-Otaño et al., 2016; Sarker et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2015; Yuan et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Marco et al., 2013; Marco et al., 2018.

claims.claim: GluN3A-NMDARs selectively and negatively regulate synaptic mTORC1-dependent translation without affecting neuron-wide transcriptional activation.
claims.source: Here, we report that GluN3A-NMDARs selectively and negatively regulate synaptic mTORC1-dependent translation without affecting neuron-wide transcriptional activation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data including RNAseq showing no transcriptional differences and biochemical data showing reduced mTOR signaling.

claims.claim: The negative regulation of mTORC1 by GluN3A is mediated by inhibition of the assembly of mTOR complexes that contain GIT1 and Raptor.
claims.source: The negative regulation is mediated by inhibition of the assembly of mTOR complexes that contain the postsynaptic adaptor GIT1 (G-protein-coupled receptor kinase-interacting protein) and Raptor.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation experiments showing GluN3A prevents GIT1/mTOR/Raptor complex formation.

claims.claim: GIT1/mTORC1 complexes are located at or near synaptic sites.
claims.source: GIT1/mTORC1 complexes are located at or near synaptic sites, and couple mTORC1 kinase activity to synaptic stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by proximity ligation assay data showing GIT1/mTOR complexes in dendritic spines.

claims.claim: GIT1/mTORC1 complexes couple mTORC1 kinase activity to synaptic stimulation.
claims.source: GIT1/mTORC1 complexes are located at or near synaptic sites, and couple mTORC1 kinase activity to synaptic stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data showing increased phosphorylation of GIT1-bound mTOR after synaptic stimulation.

claims.claim: GluN3A deletion increases the availability of GIT1/mTORC1 complexes.
claims.source: Through biochemical, mouse genetics, and behavioral approaches, we further show that GluN3A deletion increases the availability of GIT1/mTORC1 complexes, boosts mTORC1-dependent protein synthesis, and facilitates long-term memory formation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data from Grin3a knockout mice showing increased GIT1/mTOR binding.

claims.claim: GluN3A deletion boosts mTORC1-dependent protein synthesis.
claims.source: Through biochemical, mouse genetics, and behavioral approaches, we further show that GluN3A deletion increases the availability of GIT1/mTORC1 complexes, boosts mTORC1-dependent protein synthesis, and facilitates long-term memory formation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by puromycin incorporation assays showing increased protein synthesis in Grin3a knockout neurons.

claims.claim: The memory enhancement by GluN3A deletion can be reversed by the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin.
claims.source: The advantage is selectively evident when mice are subjected to weak training behavioral paradigms; can be reversed by the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin; and unlike the memory enhancement seen after manipulations of general translational regulators, is not associated with deficits in memory flexibility or extinction (Shrestha et al., 2020a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing rapamycin treatment eliminates the memory advantage in Grin3a knockout mice.

claims.claim: The memory enhancement by GluN3A deletion is not associated with deficits in memory flexibility or extinction, unlike manipulations of general translational regulators.
claims.source: The advantage is selectively evident when mice are subjected to weak training behavioral paradigms; can be reversed by the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin; and unlike the memory enhancement seen after manipulations of general translational regulators, is not associated with deficits in memory flexibility or extinction (Shrestha et al., 2020a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from reversal learning and fear extinction experiments, and contrasted with cited literature.

claims.claim: Bicuculline induces robust expression of IEGs including Arc, Fos, and Zif268/Egr1 in cultured cortical neurons.
claims.source: As expected, bicuculline induced a robust expression of IEGs implicated in the consolidation of synaptic modifications and memories, including Arc, Fos, and Zif268/Egr1 (Flavell and Greenberg, 2008; Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Enhancing GluN3A expression largely reduced the induction of Arc and Fos proteins while Zif268 induction was unaffected.
claims.source: Enhancing GluN3A expression largely reduced the induction of Arc and Fos proteins while Zif268 induction was unaffected, indicating that GluN3A selectively inhibits specific activity-dependent signaling pathways (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: GluN3A selectively inhibits specific activity-dependent signaling pathways.
claims.source: Enhancing GluN3A expression largely reduced the induction of Arc and Fos proteins while Zif268 induction was unaffected, indicating that GluN3A selectively inhibits specific activity-dependent signaling pathways (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of GluN3A on different IEGs shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Arc, Fos, and Zif268 mRNA levels were strongly induced by bicuculline in both control and GluN3A-infected neurons with no differences in the time-courses or magnitude of induction.
claims.source: Analysis at the mRNA level demonstrated that modulation occurs downstream of gene transcription: Arc, Fos, and Zif268 mRNA levels were strongly induced by bicuculline in both control and GluN3A-infected neurons, and no differences were observed in the time-courses or magnitude of induction (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: GluN3A modulation of IEG expression occurs downstream of gene transcription.
claims.source: Analysis at the mRNA level demonstrated that modulation occurs downstream of gene transcription: Arc, Fos, and Zif268 mRNA levels were strongly induced by bicuculline in both control and GluN3A-infected neurons, and no differences were observed in the time-courses or magnitude of induction (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mRNA levels are unchanged while protein levels differ.

claims.claim: Unchanged transcription by GluN3A was in-line with intact activation of the phosphorylation of ERK1/2 and CREB.
claims.source: Unchanged transcription was in-line with intact activation of the phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK1/2) and CREB (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), the two major pathways for activity-dependent transcription (Flavell and Greenberg, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citation to Flavell and Greenberg, 2008.

claims.claim: ERK1/2 and CREB are the two major pathways for activity-dependent transcription.
claims.source: Unchanged transcription was in-line with intact activation of the phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK1/2) and CREB (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), the two major pathways for activity-dependent transcription (Flavell and Greenberg, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Flavell and Greenberg, 2008.

claims.claim: The general NMDAR antagonist APV inhibited all signaling pathways analyzed and the induction of IEGs at both mRNA and protein levels.
claims.source: By contrast, the general NMDAR antagonist D-2-amino-5-phosphonovaleric acid (APV) inhibited all signaling pathways analyzed and the induction of IEGs at both mRNA and protein levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot and qRT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claims.claim: An analogous dissociation between protein and transcript levels of a subset of IEGs was observed when GluN3A-infected neurons were stimulated with BDNF.
claims.source: An analogous dissociation between protein and transcript levels of a subset of IEGs was observed when GluN3A-infected neurons were stimulated with the neurotrophin BDNF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F), a potent inducer of gene expression at both transcriptional and translational levels (Rao et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F and citation to Rao et al., 2006.

claims.claim: BDNF is a potent inducer of gene expression at both transcriptional and translational levels.
claims.source: An analogous dissociation between protein and transcript levels of a subset of IEGs was observed when GluN3A-infected neurons were stimulated with the neurotrophin BDNF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F), a potent inducer of gene expression at both transcriptional and translational levels (Rao et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Rao et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Whole transcriptome RNAseq analyses confirmed that transcriptional responses to bicuculline or BDNF were unaffected by GluN3A expression.
claims.source: Whole transcriptome RNAseq analyses confirmed that transcriptional responses to bicuculline or BDNF were unaffected by GluN3A expression (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: GluN3A-NMDARs repress the translation of specific activity-regulated mRNAs without affecting global transcriptional programs of gene expression.
claims.source: Together these results indicated that GluN3A-NMDARs repress the translation of specific activity-regulated mRNAs without affecting global transcriptional programs of gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data from western blots, qRT-PCR, and RNAseq experiments.

claims.claim: Inhibited induction of IEGs by GluN3A was not rescued by pretreatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG-132.
claims.source: Inhibited induction of IEGs by GluN3A was not rescued by pretreatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG-132 (Figure 1E), ruling out alternative mechanisms such as enhanced proteasome-dependent degradation (Rao et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 1E and citation to Rao et al., 2006.

claims.claim: mTORC1 signaling was strongly activated by bicuculline in DIV14 cortical neurons, as shown by phosphorylation of mTOR on Ser2448 and of its downstream effectors S6K and S6.
claims.source: mTORC1 signaling was strongly activated by bicuculline in DIV14 cortical neurons, as shown by phosphorylation of mTOR on Ser2448 (a reliable readout of mTORC1 kinase activity; see Chiang and Abraham, 2005) and of its downstream effectors, the p70-kDa ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K, Thr389) and the ribosomal protein S6 (Ser240–4, Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 2B and citation to Chiang and Abraham, 2005.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of mTOR on Ser2448 is a reliable readout of mTORC1 kinase activity.
claims.source: mTORC1 signaling was strongly activated by bicuculline in DIV14 cortical neurons, as shown by phosphorylation of mTOR on Ser2448 (a reliable readout of mTORC1 kinase activity; see Chiang and Abraham, 2005) and of its downstream effectors, the p70-kDa ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K, Thr389) and the ribosomal protein S6 (Ser240–4, Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Chiang and Abraham, 2005.

claims.claim: The effects of bicuculline on mTORC1 signaling were blocked by APV and MK-801, confirming NMDAR dependence.
claims.source: The effects were blocked by APV and the NMDAR open-channel blocker MK-801, confirming NMDAR dependence in our model (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The phosphorylation of mTOR, S6K, and S6 following bicuculline treatment was significantly reduced in GluN3A-infected neurons.
claims.source: The phosphorylation of mTOR, S6K, and S6 following bicuculline treatment was significantly reduced in GluN3A-infected neurons, indicating that GluN3A interferes with synaptic mTORC1 activation (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: GluN3A interferes with synaptic mTORC1 activation.
claims.source: The phosphorylation of mTOR, S6K, and S6 following bicuculline treatment was significantly reduced in GluN3A-infected neurons, indicating that GluN3A interferes with synaptic mTORC1 activation (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced phosphorylation data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Low concentrations of rapamycin (100 nM) inhibit mTORC1 but not mTORC2.
claims.source: First, low concentrations of rapamycin (100 nM) that inhibit mTORC1 but not mTORC2 (Zhu et al., 2018), blocked Arc and Fos translation in response to bicuculline without affecting Zif268, demonstrating selective mTORC1 dependence (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Rapamycin (100 nM) blocked Arc and Fos translation in response to bicuculline without affecting Zif268, demonstrating selective mTORC1 dependence.
claims.source: First, low concentrations of rapamycin (100 nM) that inhibit mTORC1 but not mTORC2 (Zhu et al., 2018), blocked Arc and Fos translation in response to bicuculline without affecting Zif268, demonstrating selective mTORC1 dependence (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The general protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin fully suppressed Arc, Fos, and Zif268 induction.
claims.source: By contrast, the general protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin fully suppressed Arc, Fos, and Zif268 induction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Restoring mTORC1 signaling in GluN3A-infected neurons by expressing constitutively active Rheb was sufficient to normalize IEG induction.
claims.source: Second, restoring mTORC1 signaling in GluN3A-infected neurons by expressing a constitutively active form of Rheb, the main upstream activator of mTORC1, was sufficient to normalize IEG induction (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Lentiviral knockdown of GluN3A in cortical neurons enhanced mTORC1 activity.
claims.source: Conversely, lentiviral knockdown of GluN3A in cortical neurons with a validated short hairpin RNA (Kehoe et al., 2014) enhanced mTORC1 activity (Figure 3A and B) and potentiated the induction of Arc and Fos by bicuculline or BDNF (Figure 3C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 3A and B, and citation to Kehoe et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Lentiviral knockdown of GluN3A potentiated the induction of Arc and Fos by bicuculline or BDNF.
claims.source: Conversely, lentiviral knockdown of GluN3A in cortical neurons with a validated short hairpin RNA (Kehoe et al., 2014) enhanced mTORC1 activity (Figure 3A and B) and potentiated the induction of Arc and Fos by bicuculline or BDNF (Figure 3C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: Increased phosphorylation of S6K and S6 was detected in hippocampal lysates from Grin3a−/− mice relative to wild-type littermates.
claims.source: Increased phosphorylation of S6K and S6 was additionally detected in hippocampal lysates from mice lacking GluN3A (Grin3a−/−) relative to wild-type littermates (Figure 3E), confirming a role of GluN3A in limiting mTORC1 signaling in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: GluN3A plays a role in limiting mTORC1 signaling in vivo.
claims.source: Increased phosphorylation of S6K and S6 was additionally detected in hippocampal lysates from mice lacking GluN3A (Grin3a−/−) relative to wild-type littermates (Figure 3E), confirming a role of GluN3A in limiting mTORC1 signaling in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the increased mTOR signaling in knockout mice shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Full-length GluN3A rescued the enhanced mTOR activation and hyperinduction of Arc and Fos proteins by bicuculline or BDNF in Grin3a−/− cultures.
claims.source: While full-length GluN3A rescued the enhanced mTOR activation and hyperinduction of Arc and Fos proteins by bicuculline or BDNF in Grin3a−/− cultures, the GluN3A1082∆ mutant failed to do so (Figure 4B–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 4B–E.

claims.claim: The GluN3A1082∆ mutant failed to rescue the enhanced mTOR activation and hyperinduction of Arc and Fos proteins in Grin3a−/− cultures.
claims.source: While full-length GluN3A rescued the enhanced mTOR activation and hyperinduction of Arc and Fos proteins by bicuculline or BDNF in Grin3a−/− cultures, the GluN3A1082∆ mutant failed to do so (Figure 4B–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 4B–E.

claims.claim: Neither GluN3A nor GluN3A1082∆ modified the activation of ERK1/2 phosphorylation or the induction of Zif268 in Grin3a−/− neurons.
claims.source: Neither GluN3A nor GluN3A1082∆ modified the activation of other signaling pathways such as ERK1/2 phosphorylation or the induction of Zif268 in Grin3a−/− neurons (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: GluN3A and GluN3A1082∆ display similar distributions and cell surface targeting.
claims.source: Since GluN3A and GluN3A1082∆ display similar distributions and cell surface targeting (Fiuza et al., 2013), the differences we observed are unlikely to stem from altered subcellular localization.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Fiuza et al., 2013.

claims.claim: GluN3A and GluN3A1082∆ yielded similarly reduced shifts in ∆Erev relative to conventional GluN1/GluN2A NMDARs, confirming that the mutant incorporated into functional triheteromeric GluN3A-NMDARs.
claims.source: GluN3A and GluN3A1082∆ yielded similarly reduced shifts in ∆Erev relative to conventional GluN1/GluN2A NMDARs, confirming that the mutant incorporated into functional triheteromeric GluN3A-NMDARs and arguing against differences in Ca2+ permeability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Both GluN3A versions drove comparable reductions in current densities relative to conventional NMDARs.
claims.source: In addition, both GluN3A versions drove comparable reductions in current densities relative to conventional NMDARs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: No differences were found between GluN3A and GluN3A1082∆ in responses to glycine of GluN1/GluN3 receptors.
claims.source: Thus, we additionally examined whether the deletion modified responses to glycine of GluN1/GluN3 receptors taking advantage of the CGP-78608 compound (Grand et al., 2018), but no differences were found (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and citation to Grand et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The absence of ionotropic differences favored the hypothesis that the inhibition of mTOR signaling requires metabotropic interactions of GluN3A-NMDARs.
claims.source: The absence of ionotropic differences favored the hypothesis that the inhibition of mTOR signaling requires metabotropic interactions of GluN3A-NMDARs, possibly modulating its association with synaptic adaptors or scaffolds.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiology data showing no ionotropic differences.

claims.claim: GIT1 is enriched in postsynaptic compartments and binds the 33 amino acids of the GluN3A C-terminus that are required for mTORC1 inhibition.
claims.source: A leading candidate is the multifunctional adaptor GIT1. GIT1 is enriched in postsynaptic compartments and binds the 33 amino acids of the GluN3A C-terminus that we show above are required for mTORC1 inhibition (Fiuza et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Fiuza et al., 2013 and the data presented earlier in the manuscript.

claims.claim: GIT1 has been detected in mTOR immunoprecipitates from mouse astrocytes by mass spectrometry.
claims.source: Although best known for its role in actin signaling (Zhang et al., 2003), GIT1 has been detected in mTOR immunoprecipitates from mouse astrocytes by mass spectrometry (Smithson and Gutmann, 2016) though a function for this association could not be established.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2003 and Smithson and Gutmann, 2016.

claims.claim: GIT1/mTOR complexes were isolated from lysates of microdissected hippocampal and cortical tissue using reciprocal immunoprecipitation.
claims.source: Using reciprocal immunoprecipitation with GIT1 and mTOR antibodies, we isolated GIT1/mTOR complexes from lysates of microdissected hippocampal (Figure 5A) and cortical (not shown) tissue.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Raptor (but not Rictor) was identified in GIT1 immunoprecipitates.
claims.source: We chose detergent conditions that preserve mTOR interactions with Raptor and Rictor (0.3% CHAPS) to further characterize the composition of the complex, and were able to identify Raptor (but not the mTORC2 component Rictor) in GIT1 immunoprecipitates.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The GIT1-binding protein βPIX was pulled down by the mTOR antibody.
claims.source: The GIT1-binding protein and Rac1 activator βPIX was also pulled down by the mTOR antibody while the control presynaptic protein synaptophysin was not (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Phosphorylated mTOR at Ser2448 was detected in GIT1 immunoprecipitates, demonstrating GIT1/mTORC1 complex functionality.
claims.source: We additionally detected phosphorylated mTOR at Ser2448 in GIT1 immunoprecipitates, demonstrating GIT1/mTORC1 complex functionality (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: GIT1/mTOR complexes are located along dendritic shafts often localized within or at the base of dendritic spines.
claims.source: PLA puncta were present along dendritic shafts often localized within or at the base of dendritic spines (Figure 5C), suggesting that GIT1 positions mTORC1 near synaptic sites to mediate dendritic translation in response to synaptic signals.
claims.evidence: This is supported by proximity ligation assay data in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: GIT1 positions mTORC1 near synaptic sites to mediate dendritic translation in response to synaptic signals.
claims.source: PLA puncta were present along dendritic shafts often localized within or at the base of dendritic spines (Figure 5C), suggesting that GIT1 positions mTORC1 near synaptic sites to mediate dendritic translation in response to synaptic signals.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Both bicuculline and BDNF induced large increases in the phosphorylation of GIT1-bound mTOR on Ser2448.
claims.source: Both bicuculline and BDNF induced large increases in the phosphorylation of GIT1-bound mTOR on Ser2448 (Figure 5D and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5D and E.

claims.claim: The phosphorylation of GIT1-bound mTOR was much higher than phosphorylation of the total cellular mTOR pool.
claims.source: Importantly, the phosphorylation of GIT1-bound mTOR was much higher than phosphorylation of the total cellular mTOR pool (BDNF: 1.98 ± 0.38- fold increase in total lysates vs. 4.2 ± 1.15 in GIT1 immunoprecipates; bicuculline: 1.42 ± 0.15 vs. 4.63 ± 1.24), consistent with a role for GIT1 in nucleating synaptic mTORC1 activation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from immunoprecipitation experiments.

claims.claim: GIT1 plays a role in nucleating synaptic mTORC1 activation.
claims.source: Importantly, the phosphorylation of GIT1-bound mTOR was much higher than phosphorylation of the total cellular mTOR pool (BDNF: 1.98 ± 0.38- fold increase in total lysates vs. 4.2 ± 1.15 in GIT1 immunoprecipates; bicuculline: 1.42 ± 0.15 vs. 4.63 ± 1.24), consistent with a role for GIT1 in nucleating synaptic mTORC1 activation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the differential phosphorylation levels.

claims.claim: Lentiviral knockdown of GIT1 blunted the activation of mTORC1 by BDNF.
claims.source: Further evidence came from GIT1 loss-of-function experiments. Lentiviral knockdown of GIT1 blunted the activation of mTORC1 by BDNF, as shown by reduced phosphorylation of S6 and S6K (Figure 5F and G), and inhibited mTORC1-dependent protein synthesis assessed using a nonradioactive puromycin-labeling assay (SUnSET) (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 5F and G.

claims.claim: Lentiviral knockdown of GIT1 inhibited mTORC1-dependent protein synthesis.
claims.source: Further evidence came from GIT1 loss-of-function experiments. Lentiviral knockdown of GIT1 blunted the activation of mTORC1 by BDNF, as shown by reduced phosphorylation of S6 and S6K (Figure 5F and G), and inhibited mTORC1-dependent protein synthesis assessed using a nonradioactive puromycin-labeling assay (SUnSET) (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by puromycin incorporation data in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: Arc translation was reduced by GIT1 knockdown, as judged by loss of rapamycin sensitivity relative to control neurons.
claims.source: Arc translation was also reduced, as judged by loss of rapamycin sensitivity relative to control neurons, while Zif268 which is mTORC1 independent was unaffected (Figure 5F and G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 5F and G.

results.result: GluN3A-NMDARs selectively inhibit the translation of specific activity-regulated mRNAs (Arc and Fos) without affecting global transcriptional programs or the induction of all IEGs (Zif268 remains unaffected).
results.evaluation: Claims C37, C46-C49, C55-C56 collectively demonstrate that GluN3A overexpression reduces Arc and Fos protein levels while leaving Zif268 unaffected (C46), mRNA levels remain unchanged (C48), and RNAseq confirms no transcriptional differences (C55). The data from western blots, qRT-PCR, and RNAseq provide converging evidence for selective post-transcriptional regulation.

results.result: GluN3A inhibits mTORC1 signaling in neurons, as evidenced by reduced phosphorylation of mTOR, S6K, and S6 in GluN3A-overexpressing neurons, and this inhibition is responsible for reduced Arc and Fos translation.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C61-C62, C64, C66 show that bicuculline activates mTORC1 (C58), GluN3A overexpression reduces this activation (C61-C62), rapamycin blocks Arc/Fos translation (C64), and constitutively active Rheb rescues IEG induction (C66). The biochemical data and rescue experiments provide strong mechanistic evidence.

results.result: GluN3A knockdown or genetic deletion enhances mTORC1 activity and potentiates the induction of Arc and Fos in cultured neurons and in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 demonstrate that shRNA-mediated knockdown (C67-C68) and genetic deletion in Grin3a−/− mice (C69-C70) both increase mTORC1 signaling and IEG induction. The convergence of loss-of-function approaches in vitro and in vivo strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: The C-terminal domain of GluN3A (amino acids 1082-1115) is required for mTORC1 inhibition, and this effect is independent of ionotropic receptor properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73, C75-C78 show that full-length GluN3A rescues the phenotype in Grin3a−/− neurons while the GluN3A1082Δ mutant does not (C71-C72), without affecting ERK1/2 or Zif268 (C73). Electrophysiology data (C75-C77) demonstrate similar ionotropic properties between wild-type and mutant, supporting a metabotropic mechanism (C78).

results.result: GIT1 forms functional complexes with mTOR and Raptor (mTORC1) that are localized at or near synaptic sites in dendrites and dendritic spines.
results.evaluation: Claims C79, C81-C86 demonstrate GIT1/mTOR complex formation through reciprocal immunoprecipitation (C81), identification of Raptor but not Rictor (C82), detection of phosphorylated mTOR in GIT1 IPs (C84), and synaptic localization via proximity ligation assay (C85). The biochemical and imaging data converge to support the existence and localization of these complexes.

results.result: GIT1/mTORC1 complexes are activated by synaptic stimulation and are required for mTORC1-dependent protein synthesis and Arc translation.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C92 show that bicuculline and BDNF increase phosphorylation of GIT1-bound mTOR more than total mTOR (C87-C88), supporting GIT1's role in nucleating synaptic mTORC1 activation (C89). GIT1 knockdown reduces mTORC1 activation (C90), protein synthesis (C91), and Arc translation (C92). The loss-of-function data strongly support the functional requirement.

results.result: GIT1/mTORC1 complex formation is developmentally regulated and negatively controlled by GluN3A through direct binding to GIT1, which prevents GIT1 from associating with mTOR.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C100 demonstrate developmental regulation (C94-C95), premature complex formation in Grin3a−/− mice (C96), rescue by full-length but not mutant GluN3A (C97), and the proposed competitive binding model (C98-C100). The developmental time-course, genetic manipulation, and rescue experiments provide strong support for the regulatory mechanism.

results.result: GluN3A controls the developmental switch from mTORC1-independent to mTORC1-dependent protein synthesis through its interaction with GIT1.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C105 show that young neurons (DIV7-9) lack rapamycin-sensitive protein synthesis (C101), GluN3A knockdown induces premature mTORC1-dependent synthesis (C102-C103), and re-expression of full-length but not mutant GluN3A reverses this (C104). The developmental, loss-of-function, and rescue data support the proposed switch mechanism (C105).

results.result: Grin3a−/− mice show enhanced spatial learning and memory in weak training paradigms of the Morris water maze without deficits in motor function, cognitive flexibility, or perseverative behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C116 demonstrate that Grin3a−/− mice perform better in weak (2 trials/day) Morris water maze training (C111), with no motor/perceptual deficits (C112-C113), enhanced reversal learning (C114), and no perseveration (C115). The behavioral data across multiple tests support enhanced learning without unwanted side effects (C116).

results.result: Grin3a−/− mice form long-lasting associative memories in a weak conditioned taste aversion paradigm, and this enhancement is reversed by rapamycin, indicating mTORC1 dependence.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C122 show that only Grin3a−/− mice form CS-US associations in weak CTA (C119), the memory is long-lasting (C120), and rapamycin eliminates this advantage (C121), supporting mTORC1 dependence (C122). The behavioral data and pharmacological reversal provide strong evidence for the mechanism.

results.result: Adult deletion of GluN3A specifically from excitatory neurons is sufficient to enhance long-term contextual fear memory, demonstrating that adult GluN3A expression in excitatory neurons gates memory formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C129 show enhanced freezing in Grin3a−/− mice at 24 and 48 hr (C124) but not 1 hr (C125), rapamycin reversal (C126), and that adult-specific deletion from excitatory neurons (C127) but not somatostatin interneurons (C128) is sufficient. The cell-type-specific and temporally controlled genetic manipulations provide strong evidence for the locus and timing of GluN3A action (C129).

results.result: GluN3A deletion enhances fear extinction without compromising fear memory acquisition, demonstrating that GluN3A deletion facilitates rather than impairs memory updating.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C132 show similar fear acquisition (C130) but enhanced extinction (C131) in Grin3a−/− mice, supporting the conclusion that memory updating is facilitated (C132). The behavioral data demonstrate that the enhancement is specific to consolidation and extinction processes.

results.result: GluN3A negatively regulates GIT1 binding to mTOR through competitive binding, as GluN3A and mTOR bind overlapping regions in GIT1.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3, C38, C134-C135 demonstrate that GluN3A prevents GIT1/mTOR complex formation (C2-C3, C38), and this is explained by overlapping binding sites on GIT1 (C134), leading to competitive binding (C135). The biochemical data and cited structural information support the competitive mechanism.

results.result: GluN3A deletion increases GIT1/mTORC1 complex availability, boosts mTORC1-dependent protein synthesis, and facilitates long-term memory formation in a rapamycin-reversible manner without compromising cognitive flexibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 show increased GIT1/mTOR binding in Grin3a−/− mice (C41), enhanced protein synthesis (C42), rapamycin-reversible memory enhancement (C43), and intact cognitive flexibility (C44). The biochemical, protein synthesis, and behavioral data with pharmacological reversal provide comprehensive support.

results.result: Grin3a−/− mice show no differences from wild-type mice in standard (strong) training paradigms for Morris water maze and conditioned taste aversion.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110, C118 demonstrate that Grin3a−/− mice perform similarly to wild-type in standard Morris water maze (C109-C110) and standard CTA (C118). The behavioral data indicate that the memory enhancement is specific to weak training conditions.

results.result: GluN3A does not affect the major transcriptional pathways (ERK1/2 and CREB phosphorylation), and general NMDAR blockade with APV or MK-801 inhibits all signaling pathways including mTORC1.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52, C60 show intact ERK1/2 and CREB phosphorylation with GluN3A overexpression (C50), confirming these are major transcriptional pathways (C51), while APV blocks all pathways (C52), and APV/MK-801 block mTORC1 activation (C60). The data support the selectivity of GluN3A's effects.

results.result: The inhibition of IEG induction by GluN3A is not due to enhanced proteasomal degradation, and general protein synthesis inhibition with anisomycin blocks all IEG induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C57 and C65 show that proteasome inhibition does not rescue GluN3A's effects (C57), and anisomycin blocks all IEGs (C65). These control experiments rule out alternative mechanisms and confirm the specificity of mTORC1-dependent translation.

results.result: Approximately 70% of GluN3A protein is expressed by excitatory neurons and approximately 20% by somatostatin interneurons in adult hippocampus.
results.evaluation: Claim C133 is supported by biochemical analysis of cell-type-specific knockout mice shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1. This quantification is important for interpreting the cell-type-specific behavioral results.

results.result: Transgenic mice with prolonged GluN3A expression (dt GluN3A) show deficits in standard conditioned taste aversion.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 is supported by behavioral data in Figure 7D showing that dt GluN3A mice have similar saccharin preference after saline or LiCl, indicating impaired CTA memory. This provides a gain-of-function complement to the loss-of-function studies.

results.result: Background knowledge claims about memory formation, protein synthesis, mTOR signaling, and NMDAR function establish the scientific context for the study.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C36 represent established knowledge in the field, supported by appropriate citations. These claims provide the necessary background and rationale for the experimental work but do not constitute novel findings of this manuscript.

results.result: Bicuculline and BDNF induce robust expression of IEGs in cultured cortical neurons, with BDNF being a potent inducer at both transcriptional and translational levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C45, C53-C54 describe standard experimental observations about bicuculline and BDNF effects on IEG expression, supported by western blot data and citations. These are methodological validations rather than novel findings.

results.result: Phosphorylation of mTOR on Ser2448 is a reliable readout of mTORC1 activity, low-dose rapamycin (100 nM) selectively inhibits mTORC1, and Zif268 is mTORC1-independent.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C63, C93 represent methodological validations and established knowledge about mTOR signaling, supported by citations and experimental controls. These support the interpretation of the main findings but are not novel discoveries.

results.result: Literature-based claims about GIT1, GluN3A expression patterns, memory mechanisms, and translational regulation provide context for interpreting the current findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C80, C106-C108, C140-C141, C145-C147, C151-C152, C155-C157, C160-C170 are supported by appropriate citations and provide important context for the discussion. These claims help position the current work within the broader literature but do not represent novel findings of this study.

results.result: Speculative and interpretive claims about GluN3A's broader functions, mechanisms, and therapeutic potential extend beyond the direct experimental evidence.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C139, C142-C144, C148-C150, C158-C159, C171-C173 involve speculation, inference, or proposals for future work. While these are reasonable interpretations and hypotheses based on the data, they extend beyond what is directly demonstrated and would require additional experiments for full validation.
